'''Willets Point''', also known locally as the '''Iron Triangle''', is an industrial neighborhood within [[Corona, Queens|Corona]], in the [[New York City]] [[borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]]. Located east of [[Citi Field]] near the [[Flushing River]], it has been known for its [[automobile repair shop|automobile shops]] and [[wrecking yard|junkyards]]. It had a population of 10 people in 2011.

Proposals to redevelop Willets Point started after [[World War II]], but gained full traction in 2007. [[New York City Council]] members and the few residents of the area strongly opposed the original plan, leading to several years of lawsuits. In 2011, the city began a $4 billion redevelopment project to construct a retail shopping center, residential buildings with a combined 3,000 units, an entertainment complex, and a public school. The [[New York City Economic Development Corporation]]'s plan to redevelop the area was approved in 2013, and demolition of the industrial section of Willets Point began in 2016.

The new development was originally set to open in stages between 2018 and 2032. However, the redevelopment plans were changed after a New York state court blocked the construction of the shopping center. The development was re-approved in February 2018. [[Etihad Park]], a [[soccer specific stadium]] due to open for the 2027–28 Major League Soccer season, began construction on the Willets Point site with a groundbreaking ceremony in December 2024.

==Description==
Willets Point is bounded by [[Northern Boulevard]] to the north, 126th Street and [[Citi Field]] to the west, [[Roosevelt Avenue]] and [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]] to the south, and the [[Flushing River]] to the east.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2"/>{{rp|2–3 (PDF p. 2–4)}} The [[New York City Subway]]'s [[Mets–Willets Point (IRT Flushing Line)|Mets–Willets Point]] station, serving the {{NYCS trains|Flushing}}, is located at the southwest corner of the area, at Roosevelt Avenue and 126th Street.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch14">{{cite web |title=Willets Point Development: Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement; Chapter 14: Transportation |url=https://www.nycedc.com/sites/default/files/filemanager/Projects/Willets_Point_Redevelopment/Environmental_Review/FSEIS/07DME014Q_FEIS_14_Transportation.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Economic Development Corporation]] |access-date=26 April 2017 |date=March 2013}}</ref> [[New York City Bus]]'s [[Casey Stengel Depot|Casey Stengel depot]] is also in that area, as well as the Q90 bus.{{rp|124–126 (PDF p. 127–131)}} The neighborhood is part of [[Queens Community Board 7|Queens Community District 7]].<ref name="NYCPlanning">{{cite web |title=NYC Planning {{!}} Community Profiles |url=https://communityprofiles.planning.nyc.gov/queens/7 |website=communityprofiles.planning.nyc.gov |publisher=New York City Department of City Planning |access-date=April 7, 2018}}</ref>

Willets Point is zoned mostly for industrial activity.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2">{{cite web |title=WILLETS POINT Development: Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement; 2: Land Use, Zoning, and Public Policy |url=https://www.nycedc.com/sites/default/files/filemanager/Projects/Willets_Point_Redevelopment/Environmental_Review/FSEIS/07DME014Q_FEIS_02_Land_Use.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Economic Development Corporation]] |access-date=26 April 2017 |date=March 2013}}</ref>{{rp|2–5 (PDF p. 2–6)}} It has no sidewalks or sewers {{as of|2013|lc=yes}},<ref name="Carr 2013" /> and due to the area's geography and the lack of paved roads in the area, flooding is common during heavy rains.<ref name="Walsh 2008">{{Cite web |url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2008/08/iron-triangle-queens/ |title=IRON TRIANGLE, Queens |last=Walsh |first=Kevin |date=August 2008 |website=Forgotten New York |language=en-US |access-date=2017-04-09}}</ref>  The area consists mostly of auto repair shops, [[wrecking yard|scrap yards]], waste processing sites, and similar small businesses.<ref name="Angotti 2006">{{Cite web |url=http://www.hunter.cuny.edu/ccpd/repository/files/willetspoint.pdf |title=WILLETS POINT LAND USE STUDY |last1=Angotti |first1=Tom Angotti |last2=Romalewski |first2=Steven |date=April 2006 |website=[[City University of New York|cuny.edu]] |publisher=[[Hunter College]] |access-date=April 9, 2017}}</ref>{{Rp|3}} It has been described as being "post-apocalyptic" in appearance.<ref name="Carr 2013">{{cite web |url=http://www.slate.com/blogs/the_eye/2013/11/15/willets_point_queens_iron_triangle_autobody_shops_new_york_city_neighorhood.html |title=Scouting a New York City Neighborhood Where the Sidewalk Ends |date=November 15, 2013 |website=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |first=Nick |last=Carr}}</ref> A [[Hunter College]] study in April 2006 found that Willets Point was a "unique regional destination" for auto parts and repairs,<ref name="Angotti 2006" />{{Rp|2}}<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.villagevoice.com/news/0624,murphy,73505,5.html |title=Melting the Iron Triangle |last=Murphy |first=Jarrett |date=June 12, 2006 |access-date=May 13, 2007 |newspaper=The Village Voice |archive-date=August 6, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070806113452/http://www1.villagevoice.com/news/0624,murphy,73505,5.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> and that the 225 businesses in the area employed a combined 1,400 to 1,800 people at the time.<ref name="Angotti 2006" />{{Rp|2, 7}}<ref name="Walsh 2008" /> It had a population of 10 people {{as of|2011|lc=yes}}.<ref name="Bilefsky 2011">{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/03/03/nyregion/03willets.html |title=In Willets Point, Workers and a Resident Fight On |first=Dan |last=Bilefsky |date=March 2, 2011 |work=The New York Times |access-date=May 16, 2012}}</ref> The concentration of auto-repair shops resulted in the area's nickname, "Iron Triangle".<ref name="Walsh 2008" />

==History==
[[File:Willets Pt from Citi Field jeh.jpg | thumb|220x124px | right | Willets Point, as seen from Citi Field looking east (2010)]]
The area was named after the portion of Willets Point Boulevard lying west of [[Flushing River|Flushing Creek]], which flows northward past the area. Willets Point Boulevard once crossed a now-demolished bridge over Flushing Creek and continued to the Willets Point [[Cape (geography)|cape]], at the confluence of the [[East River]] and [[Long Island Sound]]. The original Willets Point is the site of [[Fort Totten (New York)|Fort Totten]] near [[Bayside, Queens|Bayside]], but over the course of the 20th century it became commonplace to apply the name "Willets Point" (derived from the street, rather than the geographical feature) to the area on the Flushing River instead.<ref name="Walsh 2008" /><ref name="Pollak 2004">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/05/30/nyregion/fyi-769592.html |title=F.Y.I. |last=Pollak |first=Michael |date=May 30, 2004 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=October 10, 2009}}</ref> The neighborhood, street, and cape's name are all derived from the Willets family,<ref name="Walsh 2008" /><ref name="Pollak 2004" /> whose land the government bought in 1857 to build Fort Totten (originally named "Fort at Willets Point"<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/lpc/downloads/pdf/reports/FORT_TOTTEN_HISTORIC_DISTRICT.pdf |title=Fort Totten Historic District Designation Report |last=Pearson |first=Marjorie |date=June 1999 |website=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]] |publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]] |access-date=April 9, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100302201459/http://www.nyc.gov/html/lpc/downloads/pdf/reports/FORT_TOTTEN_HISTORIC_DISTRICT.pdf |archive-date=March 2, 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|4 (PDF p. 7)}}).<ref name="Pollak 2004" />

The area is also referred to as "Willet Point" [sic] in the official New York State Gazetteer, maintained and published by the [[New York State Department of Health]], which includes numerous defunct hamlets and towns, some with alternate or archaic spellings.<ref name="New York State Gazetteer">{{cite web |title=New York State Gazetteer / State of New York |url=https://health.data.ny.gov/Health/New-York-State-Gazetteer/cpcx-4uew/about_data |website=health.data.ny.gov |publisher=New York State Department of Health |access-date=27 August 2025}}</ref>

[[File:Citi Field.JPG|thumb|Citi Field, which opened in Willets Point in 2009]]
[[File:SheaStadium Exterior.jpg|thumb|Shea Stadium, which was located in Willets Point from 1964 to 2008]]
By the end of [[World War II]], Willets Point was known as an area of auto junkyards. Since then, several redevelopment plans for Willets Point were proposed, but never implemented.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch1">{{cite web |title=WILLETS POINT Development: Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement; Chapter 1: Project Description |url=https://www.nycedc.com/sites/default/files/filemanager/Projects/Willets_Point_Redevelopment/Environmental_Review/FSEIS/07DME014Q_FEIS_01_Project_Description.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Economic Development Corporation]] |access-date=26 April 2017 |date=March 2013}}</ref>{{rp|1}} Before the [[1964 New York World's Fair]], [[Robert Moses]] tried to incorporate Willets Point into Flushing Meadows–Corona Park but failed when the junkyard owners hired [[Mario Cuomo]] as their lawyer.<ref name="GothamGazetteWilliams">{{cite news |title=Dreaming Of A Jets Stadium (And Junkyard Cleanup) In Queens |first=Sam |last=Williams |url=http://www.gothamgazette.com/article/environment/20040512/7/977 |newspaper=Gotham Gazette |date=May 12, 2004 |access-date=January 22, 2010}}</ref> Moses regarded the region as an "eyesore and a disgrace to the borough of Queens".<ref name="topgear">{{cite web |last1=Jones |first1=Matthew |title=Welcome to NYC's chop-shop district |url=https://www.topgear.com/car-news/classic/welcome-nyc%E2%80%99s-chop-shop-district |website=Top Gear |access-date=June 6, 2024 |date=June 20, 2014}}</ref> [[Shea Stadium]], home of the [[New York Mets]] of [[Major League Baseball]] and the [[New York Jets]] of the [[American Football League]] and later the [[National Football League]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Smith |first=Curt |author-link=Curt Smith (author) |title=Storied Stadiums |url=https://archive.org/details/storiedstadiumsb00curt |url-access=registration |year=2001 |publisher=Carroll & Graf |location=New York City |isbn=0-7867-1187-6}}</ref> was opened in 1964, the same year as the World's Fair.<ref>{{cite web |last=Barrow |first=Eric |title=Shea Stadium: Mets' first miracle |website=New York Daily News|date=2008-10-23 |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/baseball/mets/shea-stadium-mets-miracle-article-1.323934 |access-date=2017-04-26}}</ref>

After the Jets left Shea Stadium at the end of the 1983 season to play at the [[Giants Stadium|Meadowlands]], Willets Point was the proposed location for a new, 82,000-seat domed football stadium that would bring the Jets back to New York. After the Jets decided to remain in [[New Jersey]], the proposed stadium was also discussed as a potential new home for the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] of the NFL, the [[Atlanta Falcons]], and the [[New Jersey Generals]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Jets Will Remain in New Jersey |first=Gerald |last=Eskenazi |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/02/07/sports/jets-will-remain-in-new-jersey.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=February 7, 1986 |access-date=January 18, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Plans for Domed Stadium in Queens in Doubt |first=Richard J. |last=Meislin |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/04/11/nyregion/plans-for-domed-stadium-in-queens-in-doubt.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=April 11, 1987 |access-date=January 18, 2010}}</ref> By the 1990s, the Mets were looking to replace the aging Shea Stadium.<ref>{{cite news |title=Mets Unveil Model Stadium: Its Roof Moves, as Does Grass |first=Richard |last=Sandomir |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=April 24, 1998 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/04/24/nyregion/mets-unveil-model-stadium-its-roof-moves-as-does-grass.html?pagewanted=all |access-date=May 21, 2010}}</ref>

New York City Mayor [[Michael Bloomberg]] started planning for the redevelopment of Willets Point in 2002.<ref name="Bagli 2018">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/02/05/nyregion/willets-point-redevelopment-de-blasio.html |title=Rising from the Ashes, Willets Point Redevelopment Will Go Forward, City Says |last=Bagli |first=Charles V. |date=2018-02-05 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2018-02-08 |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Citi Field was originally proposed as part of [[New York City bid for the 2012 Summer Olympics|the city's bid]] for the [[2012 Summer Olympics]], which was submitted in 2005.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Levy |first1=Nicole |last2=Chiwaya |first2=Nigel |title=How NYC's Failed 2012 Olympic Bid Shaped the City We Live in Today |work=[[DNAinfo.com]] |date=August 16, 2016 |url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160816/midtown/how-nycs-failed-2012-olympic-bid-shaped-city-we-live-today |access-date=August 17, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817071131/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20160816/midtown/how-nycs-failed-2012-olympic-bid-shaped-city-we-live-today |archive-date=August 17, 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Willets Point was supposed to contain athletes' housing.<ref name="Bagli 2018" /> Even though New York City lost the bid to [[London]], the plans for Citi Field progressed anyway.<ref>{{cite news |last=Shpigel |first=Ben |url=http://bats.blogs.nytimes.com/2008/12/02/citi-field-starting-to-look-like-a-real-ballpark/?hp |title=Citi Field Starting to Look Like a Real Ballpark |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=December 2, 2008 |access-date=December 3, 2008}}</ref> Following Citi Field's completion, Shea Stadium was demolished in 2009.<ref>{{cite news |title=Demolition Takes Shea Stadium Piece by Piece |first=Richard |last=Sandomir |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/10/24/sports/baseball/24mets.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 23, 2008 |access-date=August 26, 2009}}</ref> Starting in 2009, the neighborhood was discussed as a potential site for the [[New York Islanders]] of the [[National Hockey League]] to move to, before they moved to [[UBS Arena]], adjacent to [[Belmont Park]] in 2021.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://yournabe.com/articles/2010/05/20/astoria_times/news/at_islanders_willets_pt_20100520.txt |title=New York Islanders Ponder Move to Willets Point |last=Sheets |first=Connor Adams |date=May 20, 2010 |newspaper=Astoria Times |access-date=May 30, 2010}}</ref> Willets Point is currently planned to be the home of [[Etihad Park]] for [[New York City FC]] of [[Major League Soccer]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://nypost.com/2022/07/26/mayor-eric-adams-to-approve-nycfc-stadium-for-queens-sources/ |title=Mayor Eric Adams to approve NYCFC stadium for Queens: sources |date=July 26, 2022 |last1=Kosman |first1=Josh |last2=Hogan |first2=Bernadette |website=New York Post |language=en |access-date=July 27, 2022}}</ref>

[[Hard Rock International]] and [[New York Mets]] owner [[Steve Cohen (businessman)|Steve Cohen]] have proposed building a 2,300 room [[integrated resort]] in the parking lots west of Citi Field which would include a casino and be the [[List of hotels in New York City|largest hotel in New York City]] if built. The success of this proposal is dependent on the proposal receiving a casino license.<ref>{{cite web | last=Short | first=Aaron | title=Breaking down every 2025 New York casino license bid | website=City & State NY | date=February 10, 2025 | url=https://www.cityandstateny.com/policy/2025/02/breaking-down-every-2025-new-york-casino-licenses-bid/402815/ | access-date=February 19, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Flushing Post 2024 b545">{{cite web |title=Mets Owner Steve Cohen's Metropolitan Park Plan Commits over $1B in Community Benefits If Casino Gets Green Light from State |website=Flushing Post |last=Parry |first=Bill |date=February 12, 2024 |url=https://flushingpost.com/mets-owner-steve-cohens-metropolitan-park-plan-commits-over-1b-in-community-benefits-if-casino-gets-green-light-from-state |access-date=May 14, 2024}}</ref><ref name="Parry 2024 d554">{{cite web |last=Parry |first=Bill |title=Hard Rock International CEO Pitches Metropolitan Park Opportunity with Queens Business Community |website=QNS |date=January 25, 2024 |url=https://qns.com/2024/01/hard-rock-international-ceo-pitches-metropolitan-park-opportunity-queens-business-community/ |access-date=May 14, 2024}}</ref>

==Redevelopment==
===Initial proposal and controversy===
On May 1, 2007, Mayor Bloomberg announced his administration's new plan for [[urban renewal]] in the area.  The plan called for replacing the scrapyards and industrial sites with a sustainable and affordable mixed-use development including a [[convention center]], 5,500 units of housing, {{convert|1.7|e6ft2|e6m2}} of retail, {{convert|130,000|ft2|m2}} for a school, {{convert|500,000|sqft|m2}} of office space, {{convert|150,000|sqft|m2}} Community Facility, as well as environmental remediation, installation of sewers and other infrastructure, and relocation of previous businesses. Willets Point  would create more than 5,300 permanent jobs and add 18,000 construction jobs.<ref>{{cite news |first=Karla |last=Schuster |title=All signs 'Point' to makeover |work=[[AM New York]] |publisher=Tribune New York Newspaper Holdings, LLC |page=4 |date=May 2, 2007 |quote=Calling Willets Point "another euphemism for blight", Mayor Michael Bloomberg yesterday unveiled an ambitious urban renewal plan for the gritty, industrial area near Shea Stadium that would include a major environmental cleanup and a vigorous business relocation plan.}}</ref>

On April 9, 2008, the Willets Point Industry and Realty Association (WPIRA), a group of the 10 largest business and land owners in Willets Point, filed a lawsuit in the [[Eastern District of New York|US District Court for the Eastern District of New York]] against the [[New York City|City of New York]] seeking a court order requiring the City to provide infrastructure improvements, including repairs to streets and storm sewers, installation of sanitary sewers, street lights, street signs and other services that the City had allegedly withheld for over 40 years, as well as unspecified damages for past neglect. Judge [[Edward R. Korman]] granted the City's motion to dismiss this lawsuit on November 25, 2009.<ref>{{Cite court |litigants=Willets Point Industry And Realty Association, et al. v City of New York, et al. |first=Edward R. |last=Korman |court=United States District Court, Eastern District of New York |date=November 25, 2009 |access-date=November 25, 2009 |url=http://www.nyed.uscourts.gov/pub/rulings/cv/2009/8cv1453finalmo.pdf}}</ref>

On April 21, 2008, a majority of the [[New York City Council]]'s members expressed their "adamant opposition" to the proposed Willets Point redevelopment in writing to Robert Lieber, New York City's Deputy Mayor for Economic Development.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Council Declares Willets Point Plan Dead On Arrival |first=Elizabeth |last=Benjamin |date=April 21, 2008 |access-date=October 10, 2009 |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/blogs/dailypolitics/2008/04/council-declares-willets-point.html |newspaper=Daily News |location=New York}}</ref> The "adamant opposition" letter was signed by 29 City Council members. Three days later, Queens elected officials, various union members and others rallied at a press conference on the steps of New York City Hall. The gathering was in support of having the City move forward with the proposed development of Willets Point. The rally was led by Queens Borough President [[Helen M. Marshall]]. Also in attendance were state senators [[Frank Padavan]] and [[Toby Ann Stavisky]] and Assembly Member [[Nettie Mayersohn]], and former Queens Borough President [[Claire Shulman]].

On June 30, 2008, the plan was approved with numerous conditions by Queens Community Board 7 and by the [[New York City Department of City Planning|City Planning Commission]] on September 24, 2008. The City Council held a public hearing regarding the plan on October 17 and voted on November 13, 2008, to approve the redevelopment plan, which includes the potential use of eminent domain to acquire property. Some property owners have vowed to try to stop the plan through litigation, while others voluntarily sold their property to the City during the fall of 2008 so as to avert involuntary taking of their property through eminent domain and relocation by the [[New York City Economic Development Corporation]]. On July 31, 2009, the Corporation announced plans to invest $100 million into infrastructure projects in Queens that would include development in Willets Point.<ref>{{cite news |title=Willets Point's Septic Tank Days May Be Coming to a Close |first=Elizabeth |last=Dwoskin |url=http://blogs.villagevoice.com/runninscared/archives/2009/08/willets_points.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090809113120/http://blogs.villagevoice.com/runninscared/archives/2009/08/willets_points.php |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 9, 2009 |newspaper=The Village Voice |date=August 4, 2009 |access-date=January 17, 2010}}</ref>

In March 2009, Joseph Ardizzone, the only resident of Willets Point at the time, as well several local businesses filed another lawsuit in state court. The new suit challenged the City's approval of the development plan and contending that the plan had undergone inadequate environmental review. Allegations arose in 2009 that the City of New York and its Economic Development Corporation had improperly provided funding to organizations that lobbied the City Council in favor of the Willets Point development plan.<ref>{{cite news |title=New York Paid to Lobby Itself, Group Claims |first=Ray |last=Rivera |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/08/21/nyregion/21lobby.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=August 20, 2009 |access-date=April 3, 2010}}</ref> In May 2010 the [[New York City Department of Transportation]] opened a new Municipal Asphalt Plant on Harper Street, on the north side of Willets Point.<ref>{{cite news |title=City Opens Pothole Repair Plant Near Willets Point |first=Chauncey |last=Alcorn |url=http://yournabe.com/articles/2010/05/29/queens/qns_asphalt_20100527.txt |work=NY1 |date=May 27, 2010 |access-date=May 29, 2010}}</ref>

{{wide image|Willets Point Panorama.jpg|800px|From [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]]; Willets Point is in the background and to the left is [[Citi Field]] (2010)}}

===Plan approved by City Council===
In 2011, the $4 billion redevelopment project began.<ref name="CurbedNY2016July" /><ref name="bi20170406">Garfield, Leanna (April 6, 2017) [http://www.businessinsider.com/megaprojects-new-york-city-2017-4/#the-world-trade-center-site-1 "11 billion-dollar mega-projects that will transform New York City by 2035"] ''[[Business Insider]]''</ref> The next year, the city changed the agreement to include a mall with 200 stores, as well as a 2,500-unit housing development, of which 875 would be affordable housing. This caused a change in public opinion, and many of the project's original supporters came to oppose the mall.<ref name="Bagli 2018" /> A draft supplemental [[environmental impact statement]] (EIS) was published on March 15, 2013,<ref name="WilletsPtDSEIS-Notice">{{cite web |title=WILLETS POINT Development: Draft Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement; Notice of Completion |url=https://www.nycedc.com/sites/default/files/filemanager/Projects/Willets_Point_Redevelopment/Environmental_Review/DSEIS/07DME014Q__Notice_of_Completion_of_the_DSEIS.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Economic Development Corporation]] |access-date=26 April 2017 |date=March 2013}}</ref> and a final EIS was published on August 9.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Notice">{{cite web |title=WILLETS POINT Development: Final Environmental Impact Statement; Notice of Completion |url=https://www.nycedc.com/sites/default/files/filemanager/Projects/Willets_Point_Redevelopment/Environmental_Review/FSEIS/Willets_Point_NOC_FSEIS.pdf |publisher=[[New York City Economic Development Corporation]] |access-date=26 April 2017 |date=March 2013}}</ref> At the time of the FEIS's approval, the redevelopment area consisted of four parking lots around Citi Field, as well as a "Special Willets Point District" consisting of a triangle-shaped area where most of the industry was located.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch1"/>{{rp|Figure 1.1}} On October 9 of the same year, the City Council approved the Willets Point redevelopment plan.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://newyork.cbslocal.com/2013/10/09/city-council-approves-sweeping-redevelopment-plan-for-willets-point/ |title=City Council Approves Sweeping Redevelopment Plan For Willets Point |date=October 9, 2013 |publisher=CBS New York |access-date=October 11, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/11/24/nyregion/the-end-of-willets-point.html |title=The End of Willets Point |last=Nir |first=Sarah Maslin |date=November 22, 2013 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=November 26, 2013}}</ref>

In phase 1A of the plan, which was expected to be completed in 2018, a 200-room [[hotel]] would have been constructed alongside a [[retail]] area of {{convert|30,000|ft2|m2}}, connected by an [[esplanade]] at 126th Street. There would have been a temporary 2,825-spot parking lot east of the hotel and retail area, which would host recreational events for at least half the year. Meanwhile, one of Citi Field's western parking lots would have been demolished to make room for a [[Shopping mall|mall]] with {{convert|1,000,000|ft2|m2}} of leasable retail space and up to 200 stores including [[Anchor store|anchors]]. The mall would have included a [[food court]], a [[movie theater]], and a new 2,900-spot [[Multi-storey car park|parking structure]]. Another 1,800-spot parking structure would have replaced an existing 640-spot western portion of Citi Field's South Lot south of Roosevelt Avenue.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2" />{{Rp|27 (PDF p. 31)}} Even after Phase 1A was finished, there would still be a portion of the Willets Point triangle for automotive and industrial uses.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2" />{{Rp|27–28 (PDF p. 31–32)}}

Phase 1B of the plan would have taken ten more years to build, and would have complete by 2028. The temporary 2,825-spot lot would have been gradually redeveloped into {{convert|4230000|ft2|m2}} of "residential, retail, additional hotel, office, parking, and community facility" development, as well as a public school and {{convert|6|acre|ha}} of parkland. The eastern portion of the South Lot, as well as Lot D to the east, would have been replaced with two 6-floor parking structures. This proposal for Phase 1B would have followed the same zoning map as in Phase 1A.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2" />{{Rp|28 (PDF p. 32)}} As in Phase 1A, a smaller portion of the Willets Point triangle was to remain for automotive and industrial uses.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2" />{{Rp|27–28 (PDF p. 31–32)}} Since the streets in this part of the redevelopment project slope downward, the Phase 1B development would have also graded downward toward the industrial section of the neighborhood.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2" />{{Rp|28 (PDF p. 32)}}  The Van Wyck Expressway would also have had two new access ramps to serve Phase 1B.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2" />{{Rp|29 (PDF p. 33)}}   The city allocated $66 million of their budget for the design and construction of the new ramps.<ref name="CurbedNY2016July" /><ref name="bi20170406" /><ref name="CityLand 2013">{{cite web |url=http://www.citylandnyc.org/council-approved-willets-point-development-project-modification/ |title=Council Approved Willets Point Development Project Modification |work=CityLand |date=October 14, 2013 |access-date=February 10, 2015}}</ref>

[[Housing]] would have been built as part of the second phase of the project, set to be complete by 2032. There would have been 2,490 housing units, of which 35%, or 1,000, will be [[Affordable housing|affordable]] units.<ref name="CurbedNY2016July" /><ref name="bi20170406" /><ref name="CityLand 2013" /> However, in the 2013 FEIS, the EDC stipulated that there might be up to 5,850 housing units, which would comprise a combined {{convert|5850000|ft2|m2}} of space. There would also be {{convert|1250000|ft2|m2}} of retail space; {{convert|500000|ft2|m2}} of office space; {{convert|400000|ft2|m2}} of space for a new [[convention center]]; {{convert|560000|ft2|m2}} for a hotel or hotels with a combined 700 rooms; {{convert|150000|ft2|m2}} for a [[Community centre|community center]]; {{convert|230,000|ft2|m2}} for a public school; and {{convert|8|acre|ha}} of parkland. Parking would also be expanded up to 6,700 spaces based on demand. Lot B, located between Citi Field and Roosevelt Avenue, would likely have a retail area, a parking lot, and a 10-floor office building. This would significantly alter the zoning for the area, but would also bring more economic activity into Flushing and Corona.<ref name="WilletsPtFEIS-Ch2" />{{Rp|29 (PDF p. 33)}}

=== Changes to plan ===
In 2014, [[Bill de Blasio]] replaced Michael Bloomberg as [[mayor of New York City]].  He opposed the redevelopment plan because of the lack of affordable housing, but the City Council approved the project in 2015.<ref name="Brown 2017">{{cite web |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/queens/court-rips-willets-west-project-build-mall-citi-field-article-1.3101161 |title=Court rips Willets West project to build mall near Citi Field |last=Brown |first=Stephen Rex |date=2017-04-25 |website=New York Daily News|access-date=2017-04-26}}</ref> State Senator [[Tony Avella]] and a small community group sued to stop the mall from being built.<ref name="Toure 2015">{{Cite news |url=https://www.timesledger.com/stories/2015/35/megamall_web_2015_08_28_q.html |title=City decides not to appeal ruling on Willets Point mega-mall |last=Toure |first=Madina |date=August 20, 2015 |work=TimesLedger |access-date=2018-02-08 |language=en |archive-date=February 8, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180208123714/https://www.timesledger.com/stories/2015/35/megamall_web_2015_08_28_q.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> In June 2015, a state court ruled that the mall could not be built on a parking lot in Willets Point.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/07/03/sports/baseball/near-citi-field-plans-for-willets-west-are-ruled-illegal.html |title=Near Citi Field, Plans for Willets West Are Ruled Illegal |last=Sandomir |first=Richard |date=2015-07-02 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2018-02-08 |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The developers appealed the lawsuit, but the city's government refused to join in on the appeal.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/20/nyregion/new-york-city-declines-to-fight-in-court-for-complex-near-citi-field.html |title=New York City Declines to Fight in Court for Complex Near Citi Field |last=Bagli |first=Charles V. |date=2015-08-19 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2018-02-08 |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name="Toure 2015" />

By the end of July 2016, the last auto repair shops between 38th and Roosevelt Avenues had been closed and demolition had started on the development, now priced at US$4 billion.<ref name="CurbedNY2016July">{{cite news |last1=Walker |first1=Ameena |title=Demolition is underway at site of Willets Point redevelopment |url=http://ny.curbed.com/2016/7/26/12289118/willets-point-demolition-queens |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160728134540/http://ny.curbed.com/2016/7/26/12289118/willets-point-demolition-queens |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 28, 2016 |access-date=September 1, 2016 |work=Curbed NY |date=July 26, 2016}}</ref> Most Willets Points business owners either went out of business or moved to [[Hunts Point, Bronx]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/10/07/nyregion/auto-shop-owners-forced-out-of-willets-point-struggle-to-rebuild-in-the-bronx.html |title=Auto Shop Owners Forced Out of Willets Point Struggle to Rebuild in the Bronx |last=Bagli |first=Charles V. |date=2016-10-06 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2017-04-26 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Actual construction on the Phase 1 shopping area was halted by a 2015 lawsuit, which was filed to prevent the retail area from being built in a portion of the neighborhood that is legally part of Flushing Meadows–Corona Park. The suit did not preclude any other part of Phase 1A from being built.<ref name="Brown 2017" /> The [[New York Supreme Court]], which began hearing arguments in April 2017,<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.crainsnewyork.com/article/20170425/REAL_ESTATE/170429928 |title=Court case on fate of Willets Point begins |last=Anuta |first=Joe |date=2017-04-25 |work=Crain's New York Business |access-date=2017-04-26}}</ref> ruled against the construction of the mall on June 6.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170606/corona/willets-west-citi-field-appeals-court-ruling |title=Judges Block 'Willets West' Development as Potential Abuse of Parkland |last=Honan |first=Katie |date=June 6, 2017 |website=DNAinfo New York |access-date=2017-06-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170714185440/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170606/corona/willets-west-citi-field-appeals-court-ruling |archive-date=July 14, 2017 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In February 2018, the de Blasio administration and developers came to an agreement in which 1,100 lower- and middle-class apartments, a 450-pupil school, parks, and {{Convert|6|acre|ha}} of retail space would be built.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://nypost.com/2018/02/05/de-blasio-gives-green-light-to-long-delayed-willets-point-redevelopment/ |title=De Blasio gives green light to long-delayed Willets Point redevelopment |date=2018-02-06 |last=Fredericks |first=Bob |work=New York Post |access-date=2018-02-08 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Bagli 2018" /> The new plan did not include a mall, as the original plan had. Under the agreement, the developers [[The Related Companies]] and [[Sterling Equities]] were expected to clear all toxic materials from Willets Point by 2020, and the first 500 apartments were expected to open by 2022.<ref name="Bagli 2018" /><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://therealdeal.com/issues_articles/willets-point-development/ |title=Willet be? |last=Small |first=Eddie |date=2019-04-01 |website=The Real Deal New York |language=en-US |access-date=2019-08-12}}</ref> The project was further delayed until May 2021, when the Queens Borough Board voted to allow phase 1 of the Willets Point development to proceed.<ref>{{cite web |title=First Phase of Willets Point Redevelopment Plan Gets Green Light from Queens Borough Board |website=Astoria Post |date=2021-05-12 |last=Santucci |first=Christina |url=https://astoriapost.com/first-phase-of-willets-point-redevelopment-plan-gets-green-light-from-queens-borough-board |access-date=2021-06-25}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-13 |title=Willets Point Project Moves Forward With Phase One |url=https://therealdeal.com/2021/05/13/willets-point-redevelopment-finally-moves-ahead/ |access-date=2021-06-25 |website=The Real Deal New York |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Construction ===
[[File:Nycfc site.jpg|thumb|Willets Point in May 2024, between completion of [[Environmental remediation|soil remediation]] and construction of [[Etihad Park]].]]
A [[groundbreaking]] ceremony for the project took place on June 16, 2021.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.amny.com/new-york/queens/city-breaks-ground-on-willets-point-redevelopment/ |title='This is historic': City launches Willets Point cleanup for redevelopment in Queens |last=Duggan |first=Kevin |date=June 16, 2021 |website=[[AM New York Metro]] |language=en-US |access-date=2021-06-13}}</ref> The event marked the beginning of a three-year pollution remediation project at the site.<ref>{{Cite web |first=Katherine |last=Donlevy |date=June 24, 2021 |title=Willets Pt. three-year remediation begins |url=https://www.qchron.com/editions/north/willets-pt-three-year-remediation-begins/article_3166265a-3a41-58a6-b0b9-31c6bbff3797.html |access-date=2021-06-25 |website=Queens Chronicle |language=en}}</ref> In November 2022, the [[government of New York City]] and [[New York City FC]] of [[Major League Soccer]] agreed to build a 25,000-seat stadium named [[Etihad Park]] in Willets Point. The stadium was expected to be completed in 2027.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.amny.com/sports/nycfc-and-nyc-reach-deal-soccer-stadium/ |title=Nomads no more: NYCFC and NYC reach deal on soccer stadium in Queens |date=November 15, 2022 |last=Arnold |first=Christian |website=AM New York |language=en |access-date=November 15, 2022}}</ref><ref name="nyt-2022-11-15" /> It would be part of a larger [[mixed-use development]] with a 250-room hotel and 2,500 housing units on a {{convert|23|acre|ha|adj=mid}} lot.<ref name="nyt-2022-11-15">{{cite news |last1=Rubinstein |first1=Dana |last2=Belson |first2=Ken |date=November 15, 2022 |title=New York City Reaches Deal to Build Soccer Stadium in Queens |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/15/nyregion/soccer-stadium-nycfc-willets.html |work=The New York Times |access-date=November 15, 2022}}</ref><ref name="Gerbosi 2022">{{cite web |last=Gerbosi |first=Ryan |title=Soccer stadium is centerpiece of Willets Point redevelopment plan |website=Newsday |date=November 16, 2022 |url=https://www.newsday.com/sports/soccer/nycfc/nycfc-stadium-willets-point-ngjj5cfu |access-date=November 16, 2022}}</ref> The construction of Etihad Park began in December 2024; at the time, it was planned to open in 2027.<ref>{{cite web |last=McLogan |first=Elle |title=Construction begins on NYCFC's new stadium in Queens |website=CBS New York |date=December 4, 2024 |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/construction-begins-etihad-park-new-york-city-fc-soccer-stadium-queens/ |access-date=December 5, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=O'Brien |first=Shane |title=NYCFC breaks ground on Etihad Park, NYC's first soccer-specific stadium, in Willets Point |website=QNS |date=December 4, 2024 |url=https://qns.com/2024/12/nycfc-breaks-ground-on-etihad-park-nycs-first-soccer-specific-stadium-in-willets-point/ |access-date=December 5, 2024}}</ref><ref>[https://www.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/877-24/mayor-adams-councilmember-moya-new-york-city-football-club-break-ground-new-soccer-stadium- "Mayor Adams, Councilmember Moya, New York City Football Club Break Ground on new Soccer Stadium, Etihad Park, in Willets Point"], [[Mayor of New York City]] press release dated December 4, 2024. Retrieved December 4, 2024. "New York City Mayor Eric Adams, New York City Councilmember Francisco Moya, Queens Borough President Donovan Richards, and the New York City Football Club (NYCFC) today officially broke ground on Etihad Park, New York's first professional soccer-specific stadium and Major League Soccer's (MLS) first fully-electric stadium across the nation. In addition to the stadium – which will be operational by the 2027 MLS season and is being entirely privately financed by NYCFC – this project will also deliver retail, food and beverage facilities, office space, and 'City Square,' a plaza for community uses and events."</ref> The two residential buildings in the first phase of Willets Point's redevelopment were halfway completed in January 2025<ref>{{cite web |last=Marshall |first=Ethan |date=January 8, 2025 |title=First phase of Willets Point redevelopment reaches construction halfway mark – QNS |url=https://qns.com/2025/01/first-phase-willets-point-beyond-halfway/ |access-date=May 5, 2025 |website=QNS}}</ref> and [[topped out]] that May.<ref>{{cite web |last=Gillespie |first=Max |date=May 4, 2025 |title=Phase One Of Willets Point Progresses In Willets Point, Queens |url=https://newyorkyimby.com/2025/05/phase-one-of-willets-point-redevelopment-tops-out-in-willets-point-queens.html |access-date=May 5, 2025 |website=New York YIMBY}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
The "Valley of Ashes" described in [[F. Scott Fitzgerald]]'s novel ''[[The Great Gatsby]]'' is said to have been inspired by a former dump (now the location of [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]]) in Willets Point.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wnyc.org/story/216534-blog-mayor-valley-ashes-great-gatsby-was-inspired-willets-point/ |title=Mayor: Valley of Ashes in 'Great Gatsby' Was Inspired by Willets Point |date=June 14, 2012 |publisher=WNYC |access-date=December 11, 2013}}</ref> The 2007 film ''[[Chop Shop (film)|Chop Shop]]'' was also filmed and set in this neighborhood.<ref>{{cite news |first=Nathan |last=Lee |title=Chop Shop: A Kid's Rundown Queens |url=http://www.villagevoice.com/2008-02-26/film/king-of-queens/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080915192055/http://www.villagevoice.com/2008-02-26/film/king-of-queens/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 15, 2008 |newspaper=The Village Voice |date=February 26, 2008 |access-date=September 3, 2009}}</ref> The 2010 dramatic film ''Willets Point'', directed by T. J. Collins, is set in the neighborhood.<ref>Catsoulis, Jeanette (November 25, 2010) [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/26/movies/26roundup-willets.html "Latino Family Drama:] ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>

The 2018 documentary ''The Iron Triangle'', directed by Prudence Katze and William Lehman, describes the history behind the destruction of the once-thriving neighborhood.<ref>Kensinger, Nathan (February 22, 2018) [https://web.archive.org/web/20180222205724/https://ny.curbed.com/2018/2/22/17038794/willets-point-queens-development-photo-essay "The Life and Death of Willets Point"] ''[[Curbed|Curbed New York]]''</ref>

The 2010 [[cinéma vérité]] documentary ''Foreign Parts'' is shot in Willets Point and shows life and industry there prior to redevelopment.
